[Success! Homage to the All-Knowing One. Here, in order to cause wonder in the wise, the question is posed in three ways: by means of the interrogative pronoun *kiṃ*, by means of a request for an explanation, and by means of intonation (*kāku*). The answer is twofold: external and internal. That which is contained within the very verse of the question is the internal; the other is the external. First is the play of the distributed and the collective; its definition is as follows: where first the question is asked part by part, and afterwards not part by part.
They say that this question-and-answer is twofold, known as "separate" (*vyasta*) and "combined" (*samasta*). 1. External (*bāhya*). 2. Sentence (*vākya*).
What indeed is the nature of the *haṃsa*-family, known as both distinct and collective?
Whom did the enemy of Kaṃsa steal away from the Yamunā?
Or who, unless he is a Sugata, knows the profound greatness of the Sugata? (1)

[Commentary: *Haṃsa*. The word *vā* means "or. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Whom does the Sugata (the Well-Gone One) not know? because of his profundity? His "well-gone" (*sugata*) nature refers to the lineage of swans (*haṃsakula*). The "serpent" (*ahi*) here is the Naga Kāliya; his pride—that is, his arrogance—was subdued by him in the pool of the Yamunā. The "majesty" (*mahimā*) of the Sugata is his greatness. It has reached the culmination of increase and purity, consisting of the perfection of supreme qualities. No one other than the Buddha knows that, just as a frog in a well cannot know the majesty of the ocean.
Which [vowel] ends a class? Whose song is distinguished? What is that braid of hair? And who are those two locks of hair? Who are those two?
For whom are Keśava and Īśa the lords of the two [deities] Moma and Maya, who are both skilled in destroying the enemies of the gods? (2)
The subsequent section on the fragments.

[Commentary: What is a *varga*? A *dhammilla* is a particular arrangement of hair; *kuntala* and *alaka* are synonyms. These three terms may be used individually. Or, it refers to the final letter of the *ma*-group (*ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*). Or, it is the final letter of the *pa*-group (*pa*, *pha*, *ba*, *bha*, *ma*). Regarding *maya*: for a *kiṃnara*, the *dhammilla* and *kuntala* are the "arrangements" (*veśa*) of the hair. It is called *veśa* because it enters (*viśati*) [the head]; it is an adornment. An *arrangement of hair* (*keśaveśa*) is an ornamentation that is a modification of the hair. *Mā* is Lakṣmī. [Curl. A single part of a verse that is neither a quarter-stanza (*pāda*) nor a half-verse is a *khaṇḍa*;
therefore, an answer consisting of such a part is a *khaṇḍottara*. [Curl. Call upon the dull-witted Indra, the mountain, Umā, and the ornaments of milk-drops.

"Call out! The dull-witted one is ignorant; the lord is the sun. These four are scattered: *manda*, *rave*, *aga*, *bhavāni*.
When an enemy approaches, let the one with a withered army be spoken of; and when the planet is retrograde, let the giver of horses be spoken of."
Let the lotus-handed Avalokiteśvara, who possesses supreme compassion and is intent on the welfare of others, be invoked. || 4 ||

[Commentary: *Ripū* (enemy). One whose army has gone to withering is *śuṣkacamūkaḥ*. Regarding *vakragate*: "in a crooked course. *Vyaste dve* (two are separated). *Parodayāvānabalaḥ*: *paraḥ* means enemy; *udayaḥ* is rising; by that, *āvānabalaḥ* is one whose strength is diminished (*śuṣkacamūkaḥ*). From the root *ovai* (to wither), preceded by the prefix *āṅ*; the change to *na* occurs in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), hence *āvānam*. *Aka* / *aga*: in the sense of crooked motion. In *akite*, it means having moved crookedly. *Aśvaraḥ*: one who gives a horse (*aśvam rāti iti aśvaraḥ*). From the root *rā* (to give) [in the sense of giving].
[In the sense of giving: the suffix *ka* is applied. He who is supremely compassionate is the most merciful.
"O son of the Wind, speak! I am filled with various kinds of rice," he cried out, enchanting the beloved of the enemy of Smara (Śiva).
Speak, Mañjuśrī, you who pacify; mindful, you scatter the entire web of delusion; meditated upon, O Mañjughoṣa! || 5 ||
[The commentary explains: "Speak!

The three [words] are separate: *kir*, *asi*, and *kaḥ*. *Kaḥ* means the wind (*pavana*). *Kiḥ* is its offspring (*apatyam*). *Asi* means you are (*bhavasi*). I am *sakalamaḥ*; *kalamaḥ* is a specific kind of rice. What [being], of what sort, torments the king? What [being], of what sort, torments the king? *kā kīdṛk kaṣati nṛpam*?
"O Lord, tell me, what does the moon say to me at night?
O Jina, let it be told;
she is born of rays, she bestows liberation, and she is victorious. (6)
Victorious is Mārīcī, the remover of existence!

*Bhavaharā jayati* (Victorious is she who removes worldly existence). [The commentary explains: *Kaṣati* means "it grinds" or "it afflicts. *Niśi yat khaṃ tad āha* ("It speaks of that which is the sky at night") refers to the moon. *Kiṃ karoti māṃ candraḥ* ("What does the moon do to me? is a question regarding an action. The four words are separated: *mā*, *arīcī*, *bhavaha*, *rājayati*. *Arīcī*: one who moves toward enemies (*ari*). The meaning is "the fortune that has gone to the enemy. *Bhavaha*: one who carries the stars (*bhāni*); here the suffix *ac* is applied. O *Bhavaha*! In the compound form, there are three words: *Mārīcī*, *Bhavaharā*, *Jayati*. She is born from rays (*mayūkha-jā*) and originates from rays (*marīci-bhavā*); therefore, by name she is *Mārīcī*.

Since she bestows liberation, she removes worldly existence; since she is victorious, she conquers. [Whispered: "What bitter thing would you say? What white thing? And what is the news of your husband? O Queen, tell me the way in this indirect manner.
O Jina, those words of yours are to be proclaimed; O Śākyamuni, they lead one to the right method.

"Speak *kaṭvīm*—speak what is pungent (*kaṭukām*). Who is *dhavalā*? Who is the husband (*pati*)? What is the news (*vātī*)? The meaning is 'the wife of the wind' (*vātasya bhāryā*). *Nayattā* is the state of leading (*nayana*), that is, leadership (*netṛtva*). These five words are separate: *vacām*, *sitā*, *kīśā*, *kī*, and *amunena yanti*. Your words lead; they bring the world to its rise and its end. [Note added in the upper margin of the manuscript: "By this manner, it is said: 'by him' (*amunā yathā*)."]
"What kind of person is one who releases [others], and what kind is one who does not? At what kind of offense do they become angry?
Call out separately: 'this vehicle,' 'the tree,' and 'the two shoulders.'"

Indeed, for how many times, for what purpose, of what kind, and where have even men held the tips of the soles of the Victors' feet upon their heads? What is the desired happy rebirth, prosperity, or reputation that results at the end?
Even once, when the dust from the feet of the Sugata has been borne upon the head.

What does the chaff do to the rice-grains? [It is] threshed with pestles. What is the husk? [It is] firm. Where was the moon born? [In] the ocean. What was done by the powerful one? [He] held up the mountain. What does a man carry in battle?
[He carries] a sword. What is done with mouths? [They are used for] speech. O Jina, tell me the glory of the Jina that pervades the three worlds. 10.

What is powerful? What is the burden (*bhara*)? Where? What is the suffix *tuk*? What does it do? Was it done? Is it being done? In these three questions, the word "does" (*karoti*)—which expresses action in general—is not used because there is no connection [to a specific agent]. A specific action is asked about, not a substance; therefore, a verb is the answer to these. Ten [words] are scattered: *nādaḥ*, *pāt*, *arajaḥ*, *avahanti*, *śi*, *rasā*, *ke aśāki*, *asiṃ*, *hasyate*.

What is sound? *Nādaḥ* (sound). The root *pā* means "to protect"; with the suffix *śatṛ*, the elision of *s* (*sor luk*), and the form *pāt* (protecting), it refers to those who protect. Born from those who protect is *arajaḥ* (dustless). By the rule *śi śakāre śi tug*, when the suffix *śi* follows the letter *ś*, the augment *tuk* is added. *Rasā* is the earth. *Ke* means water. Having done what, where, by whom, and of what nature would those rays born from the smiling face of the Jina—how many and which ones—illuminate the ten directions at the end of the age, their purpose indicated by the disappearance of the Blessed One’s physical remains? (11)

[Commentary: What is it like? "Haritaśamaḥ" means the subsiding of young grass. "Having done what?"—this is a question regarding an action. "Smite" refers to the Jina who has a slight smile. There are six [words] used distributively (*vyasta*). "Udbhāsyā. "Śādaśānte. "Bhagavat. "Apaghanāntā. "By means of supernatural powers (*ṛddhibhiḥ*). "Sūcitārtham. "Udbhām" means one whose face or mouth has risen stars; she is "udbhāsyā. "Śāda" means young grass. "Bhaga" means the sun. "Apaghanāntā" means that from which the density (*ghana*) has departed at its two ends; thus [it is called]. "Suṣṭhu" (well).

It has a fitting meaning; it indicates a profound meaning. It is both singular and comprehensive. For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are always in a state of meditative equipoise; they smile only on rare occasions, when they desire to explain some specific matter to someone.

And then, blue, yellow, red, and white rays of light issued forth from their mouths; having illuminated the ten directions and accomplished the welfare of sentient beings in those quarters, they returned and dissolved into some part of the Blessed One’s body, indicating some matter that was to be prophesied. For when the Blessed One desired to prophesy the rebirth of someone in the hells, those rays would dissolve into the sole of the Blessed One’s foot.

When [he wishes to prophesy rebirth] among animals, it vanishes into his heel; when among hungry ghosts (*preta*), into his big toe; when among humans, into his two knees; when among gods, into his navel; when wishing to prophesy the state of a powerful wheel-turning monarch (*balacakravartin*), into the palm of his left hand; when [the state of] a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), into his right hand; when [the awakening of] a disciple (*śrāvaka*), into his mouth; when [the awakening of] a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*), into the circle of hair between his eyebrows (*ūrṇā*); when [perfectly complete awakening] (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), it vanishes into his uṣṇīṣa at the very end.
The limbs are the secondary members (*apaghana*). The *antardhayaḥ* are the concealments (*antardhānāni*).

"Tell me, friend, which of these four positions do you choose in battle— one that shakes two peaks of excellence, or one that grants safety from fear? "Tārā."
The essence, the strength, both of these, and the purifier. || 12 ||

"Thou wert [the means for fearlessness] in battle. For the sake of fearlessness—fearlessness being the weapon (or method)—five words are used separately: *āsam*, *sāram*, *bharam*, *ubhayam*, and *dhōtāram*. From the root *as* (to be), the form *āsam* is derived with the substitution of *am* for the *tiṅ* suffix *mip*. *Sāra* means strength (*balam*). *Dhōtā* means a shaker (*kampayitā*). One word is combined according to the Prakrit rule. *Bhayandha* means blinded by fear; being one whose vision is lost through fear, may I remember the Blessed Lady intensely (*tāram*) as the bearer (*bharamu*). In the case of the root *smṛ* (to remember), there is the substitution of *bhara* for *bharāmu*. *Ā saṃsāram* means as long as cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) lasts."

Who is the son of Daśabala? Who is Dāma?
O you who accept the offering of the moon from the Lord of the Gods as a token of love, we bow before you. || 13 ||

[Commentary: *Āhva* means "wine" (*madhu*). *Utsavasaṃjña* means "festival" itself. *Daśabalaha* means "from the Ten-Powered One" (*daśabalāt*). *Lahiru* means "obtained. *Kasu* means "of whom" (*kasya*); the meaning is "of what kind? *Dāmaha* means "of a bond" (*dāmnaḥ*). *Akusumaha* means "of one without flowers" (*akusumasya*), that is, "of one devoid of blossoms. [The commentary explains: "To be entreated" (*yācyaḥ*). "Addressing" (*āhvā*) means calling out. "He would accept" (*abhyupeyāt*) means he would agree to it. "Or else" (*yadvā*) has the sense of "alternatively" (*athavā*). "Protection" (*guptiḥ*) is derived from the root *gup* (to protect) with the suffix *ktin*. "Of the subjects" (*prajānām*) refers to the gods and others. "One" (*ekaḥ*) means without a second. "Superior" (*śreyān*) means foremost. "Benefactor" (*arthakartā*) means a doer of good; a kinsman (*bāndhavaḥ*). [The following words] are fourteen when taken separately: *rakṣāmūḥ*, *dhanyam*, *oghāḥ*, *bhavasabha*, *yamarut*, *nāgamartyāḥ*, *surāṇām*, *buddhasya*, *ekāgrabandhaḥ*, and *arjayati*.

The lotus-line on the feet of the Blessed One is excellent and minute. "Bhavasaṃbha" is a collection of those who are *bhava*s (or Rudras); its neuter gender is due to the rule regarding words ending in *a* when preceded by *na*. A "Yamarut" is one who restrains Yama, because of warding off death. Regarding "nāgamartya": *nā* means a person; he knows the Dharma through the attainment (*ṛti*) or knowledge of the Āgama. Regarding "of the Buddha": of the known reality. "Samādhi" means the binding or restraint of the mind upon a single point of focus (*ālambana*).

[The word *arjayati*] refers to a person who acquires [merit]. *Bhaga* is the Sun; by him, [the Sun], he was entreated (*vata*). [The suffix] *kta* is applied to the root *vanu* (to entreat). *Pāda* means rays; their *rājī* is a row. *Vare* means a son-in-law. *Ekaṃ samastam*: the dust of the lotus-feet of the Blessed Buddha is victorious. Of what kind? Of him who is the sole-pointed friend (*ekāgrabandhu*), the peerless and excellent friend of sentient beings. That dust which, remaining upon the head, becomes an unfailing protection for those in existence (*bhava*) who are beset by fear—namely, the gods, nāgas, mortals, and asuras. {[Curl]} }

There are nine individual [words]: *surava*, *raseha*, *ramaṇi*, *moha*, *māsa*, *lāḥ*, *māḥ*, *rave*, *rīṇa*. *Rasāyām* (in the earth) *īhā* (desire) belongs to him; thus he is *raseha*. *Lāḥ* means light syllables (*laghu*), because in the science of prosody (*chandaḥśāstra*) the designation *la* is prescribed for a light syllable. *Māḥ* means Soma. *Rīṇaḥ* means melted or flowed away; it is the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *rīṅ* (to flow), with the change to *na* according to the rule *oditaś ca*. The whole [compound] is as follows: [He whose desire is for the earth, whose light syllables are like the moon, and from whom [the darkness] has flowed away.]

The meaning is: "the radiance of the toe-nails of the Buddhas, the enemies of Māra, which is thick with the rays of the crest-jewel of the best of gods. Regarding the words *mayūra* (peacock) and *mayūkha* (ray), by the rule *vāyv-eti*, the vowel *au* is substituted for the preceding vowel. By the rule *khaghathadhabhāṃ haḥ*, [the *ha* is applied]. In *moha*, by the rule *māṃsādiṣu vā*, there is optionally the elision of the *anusvāra*. [Thus] *māsa*. [Curl] || The preceding vowel becomes *au*. [Commentary: "Tat" refers to that which is denoted by the word *tat*. *Ācāma* is the liquid of rice being cooked. *Gardha* is thirst. *Aṇḍaja* is a bird. This is a *dvandva* compound in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). Those two whose water originates from Acyuta are to be designated [as such]. *Jñāna* is knowledge (*vidyā*). *Atyarthadāna* is excellent giving. Regarding "ānathuḥ": from the roots *śvas* (to breathe) and *ana* (to breathe). The meaning is: "Have you both breathed? This is a question posed with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*). *Valaya* means a circle. *Moha* itself is the darkness (*dhvānta*).

The sun consists of knowledge; he is the progenitor of knowledge. The word *iva* is used in the sense of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). The word *vā* means "or. The thirteen syllables are distributed as follows: *sa*, *prabha*, *a*, *maṇḍalo*, *bhāti*, *jaḥ*, *inaḥ*, *ajāmbūnadadyutiḥ*, *ajñānatimirārātiḥ*, *jñāḥ*, *nadīdhitim*, *āniva*. Regarding *sa*: there is an elision of the vocative case-ending after that which is denoted by the pronoun *tat*. *Atiḥ* means a hawk. *Ajāta* means unborn (*aja*). *Nada* means the Śoṇa river. Its *dyutiḥ* (splendor) is its approach.

[The word *dyu* means] approaching; [the suffix] *ktin* [is used here]. *Ajñānatim* means the service of the ignorant; *ajñā* means service. *Irā* is the earth. *Dhitiḥ* means supporting; from the root *dhī* in the sense of supporting, [the form] *aniteḥ* [is derived] with the suffix *liṭ*, [followed by] *vas*, and the substitution of *v* [for *u*]. The entire [explanation] is easy to understand. [Note: The reading *ānathuḥ* is supported by the manuscript (*ānathu(che)r*), while the edition reads *ānathuḥ*.
The term *inaḥ* has been emended by the editor; the manuscript reads *ilaḥ*.]

And for this reason, they alone have given much to me, but I have not [given] to them. [The fourteen Prakrit words are: *matto*, *vi*, *tavanto*, *janta*, *vora*, *savahaṃ*, *bhavebha*, *vesā taṃ*, *buddhohante*, *nāyaṃ*, *te*, *vahu*, *dāvaṃ*, *dhavo*, *nāham*. Their meaning is: *matto* (from me), *api* (even), *tapan* (O scorcher), *he yān* (O you who go), *he badara* (O jujube tree), *svapatham* (your own path), *bhavasya ibha* (the elephant of existence), *veśyā tvam* (you are a courtesan), *buddhaughānte* (at the end of the flood of Buddhas), *jñātam* (known), *tava* (of you).

He [is] the bridegroom (*vadhū*), the forest (*vana*), the husband (*dhava*), the protector (*nātha*). Awakening (*bodha*) is the Buddha; the flood (*ogha*) of that [awakening]; at its end (*tasyānte*). Or else, at the end of the flood of awakening (*buddhyoghānte*): in the case of the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) of the letter *i*, there is elision according to the rule "the elision of vowels (*ajlopa*) is variously applied. In the word *jñāta* (known), the *na* replaces *jña*. Regarding the letter *ta*, since the rule "there is generally elision of *ka, ga, ca, ja, ta, da, pa, ya, va*" would apply, it is here permanently [retained]. In the case of *kabandha*, since the rule "in the middle of the six vowels, *ya* is optionally substituted" applies, there is an option for the substitution of *ya*. For example: *cayabhāya*, *vayaṇa*, *raya*.

In the *naya* [section] and those that follow, in due order: "entirely" means in the *saṃskṛta* language. "In birth after birth," "beings," "sāta" means happiness (*sukha*), "rasavahaṃ" means endowed with flavor (*svāduyukta*). "From me" means from my presence. "Have obtained" (*avitavantaḥ*) means they have attained; here the root *avi* has the sense of attainment. This is because the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*) states: "The root *avi* is used in the senses of protection, going, satisfaction, understanding, entering, hearing, ownership, begging, buying, desire, shining, obtaining, embracing, burning, existence, and increase."

[Commentary on Śrīśā: The "Unborn" (aja) is Viṣṇu; the "Other Unborn" (ananya-aja) is Rāhu. For what reason does Rāhu pierce me? There is no connection [between him] and Yatnaśrī, the daughter of Yatnaśīla. They "go" (yānti), meaning they attain. The four [syllables] are scattered. By means of the four feet, according to the doctrine of Yoga and others: *i*, *o*, *aga*, *ādi*, *mate*, *ana*, *na aḥ*. O *ana*! By the son of Māyā—Mā being the moon (*candra*), his daughter is Māyātanayā. O *ina*!

For thus, on the new moon day (*amāvasyā*), the sun and the moon dwell together. Therein, they say that through the swallowing (*grāsa*) of the nectar-filled moon, there occurs the swallowing of the sun; this is according to the view of the *Yogādis*. *Ī*, *aḥ*, *agāt*, *viṣṇur agamat*. According to the view of *Imata*—that is, the view of *Kāma*—the word *mata* has the sense of "desire. From the root *yat* with the suffix *yuc*, we have *yatanaḥ*, meaning "one who exerts effort" (*yatnaśīla*). His descendant is *yātaniḥ*. For him, there is neither *mā* nor *śrī* (fortune). This is the complete [meaning]. He who has been proclaimed (*agādi*) by the speaker (*gadika*). According to the established view (*matena*). According to what is well-known (*prasiddhena*).

"By the son of Māyā" means by the son of Queen Māyā; "not by him," meaning not by another than he. "By *naya*" means by policy, by method. "*Yoga*" is meditative absorption (*samādhi*); its "beginning" is its commencement. "Do not go" means do not reach it, do not perform it—the sense being that the very performance of the commencement is itself the reaching of it. He asks: if this follows the verse, why is it treated separately? He replies: "It is a half-verse repetition. A "half-verse repetition" (*ardhābhyāsa*) is a difficult type of *yamaka* (chiasmus).

And what kind of thought arises in an elephant that has entered a forest of *śallakī* trees? (33)
And five or six branches.

[Commentary: "Ask. The companions of lovers are the *viṭa*, the *vidūṣaka*, the *pīṭhamarda*, and the *ceṭa*. "Five or six" (*pañcaṣāṇi*) means five or six; the suffix *ḍac* is applied to form the compound. Kumārila previously declared that Jaimini taught six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Later, Prabhākara stated there were five, excluding non-existence (*abhāva*). A *viṭapa* is a branch or a stalk. *Caṣāṇi*—the root *caṣ* meaning "to eat" is used in the imperative (*loṭ*); the suffix *mer* is added, and *āṭ* is inserted before the first person singular ending. [The verse remains untraced.]
"Let Gandhāra be told to perform [the rite] for the Skyclad One (Śiva); Nārada knows of that great sacred ford where the waters of two rivers mingle. (34)
Of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
[Commentary: *Gandhā* [means] "for the sake of Kṛttivāsas" (Śiva); "arthe" is to be supplied. *Gaṃ* means "O Sage, sing. *Oḥ* [is an interjection]. *Gam* thus refers to *Gāndhāra*.
Who is called what by the Śaivas? And who is the festival for the eyes of the gods? *Urvaśī*.
Who is to be avoided? Those who consume sesame seeds. Or what is it that deludes the vision of the gods? [The consumption of sesame seeds. 35.
Tilottamā.

Who? *uḥ* is Śaṅkara; he is the self-controlled one (*vaśī*), capable of accomplishing everything by his mere will. *Urvaśī* is a celestial courtesan (*devaveśyā*). [Vāryā: When the suffix *kap* is applied to the sense of "oiliness" (*snehanam*) of sesame, it becomes *tilāḥ*; when the suffix *kvip* is applied, it becomes *tilaḥ*, meaning "sesame seeds. *Atta mā* means "do not eat. *Tilottamā* is a celestial courtesan (*suragaṇikā*).
Who is obstructed? Who are obstructing? Who are the white ones in the city that admit strangers?
Even if a thunderbolt were to fall upon a grove, what would it be compared to a plowshare? (36)
The subsequent section on the fragments.

[Commentary: *Kā ru* means "who blocks" or "who obstructs," that is, who prevents. Likewise: *ke rundhanti* ("who block"?), *kiṃ ruṇaddhi* or *ruddhanti* ("what blocks"?). To this he replies: *parapavesaṃ purammi* ("the entry of others into the city"). Thieves, rival kings, and so forth—these are the ones whose entry into the city is blocked. Thus there are two questions. "Who are the white ones? These three [questions] are in Prākrit, while the fourth is in Saṃskṛta. The answer begins with "ārāma" and so on; the answer is *phalihā*. In the first sense, it means a moat (*parikhā*).

In the second [verse], *parighāḥ* refers to the bolts of the city gates. In the third, *sphaṭikāḥ*. In the fourth, *phalihā* means those who strike fruit-bearing trees (*phalinaḥ vṛkṣān*). Regarding the two instances of the letter *pa* becoming *pha* in *puruṣaparighaparikhāsu*, it is according to the rule *paruṣa* [becomes] *pha*. Regarding the change of the letter *ra* to *la* in *haridrādīnāṃ ro laḥ*, it is the substitution of *la* for *ra*. Regarding the substitution of *ha* for *kha* and *gha* in *khaghathadhaphabhāṃ haḥ*, it is the substitution of *ha* for *kha* and *gha*. Regarding the elision of the upper [vowel] in *uparilopaḥ kagaḍatadapaṣasām*, there is the elision of *sa* in *sphaṭike*. Regarding the substitution of *la* for *ṭa* in *sphaṭike laḥ*, it is the substitution of *la* for *ṭa*.

In the case of *sphaṭikanikaṣacikureṣu*, why is there the substitution of *ha* for *ha*? In the rule *jasśasor lopaḥ*, when *jas* is elided, the rule *jasṅasibhyasāmsu dīrghaḥ* effects the lengthening of the vowel *a*. From the word *parikhā*, by the rule *antyahalaḥ*, there is the elision of the suffix *su*.
[Curly mark] These three are connected and sung among the three vowels; which syllable is what?
And they declare that the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean is a sacred ford (tīrtha). || 37 ||

In this context, no distinction is made between the *anusvāra* and the fifth [consonant of the class]. [Commentary: Regarding the vowels: *gaṃ*, *gā*, *sā*, *gara*, *saṅgamaṃ*. These are associated with the three notes (*svara*)—*ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, and *madhyama* (the *gāndhāra* being included). If it is argued that there is an impossibility of the vowel *a* occurring after *ga*, and furthermore that *ga* is redundant, we say: no. For in dance and other arts, the word *gāndhāra* is also sung; having omitted its middle syllable, the word *gara* is used here. Therefore, there is neither impossibility nor redundancy, because *ga* is distinguished by its presence or absence in the compound.

[Objection: But surely, in the first [verse] there is *gaṃ* and *maṃ*, while in the second there is *ṅam*; how then can there be equality? To this he replies with the words beginning "anusvāra" (*anusvāra-ityādi*). This is merely an illustration; for in this context, even the distinction between *vac* and so forth is certainly not taken into account. What instrument, generally accompanied by speech, causes one to hear? Of what kind is that penance which, together with its weightiness, destroys sin? (38)

"What, what? What instrument and what conversation does it mostly make audible, and what syllable? Yet these very things do not make them audible, because of the extreme abundance of vowels and syllables. In the second [case], there are wealthy lords; among them is dignity (*garimā*), that is, weightiness (*gaurava*). Together with that, it is "possessing the dignity of wealth" (*sadhanigarima*). They consider such asceticism to be a sin, because it is something that ought not to be done.
Bowing down, by whom was he taken by Rāma while he was virtuous; and by whom, at the end of separation?"
By whom or for what reason has this state of impurity been acquired by that which is as white as crystal? || 39 ||
Lakṣmaṇa was marked by the deer-marked one.

"By whom was he seized, by what agent, with what instrument, while he was in the state of Rāma? Prostrating himself at the end of their separation—he [was seized] by Hari (Viṣṇu) with his lap (aṅka). Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, was the second. By Hari with the moon as his mark (hariṇāṅka); from Lakṣmaṇa; 'lakṣman' means a mark, the hare-mark on the moon.
"Whom has whom caused to set? 'In whom? asks Manmatha when he is enraged. She must be entreated by those who desire her to give her up, for she is exceedingly submissive to her father. (40)
O Śaṅkara, who bestows the body and the self!
"O Father, give me [the power] to bring him under my control when Śaṅkara is enraged!

[The crow: "By what kind of splendor could I take away the fortune of my enemy? What could I do? [Commentary: "When enraged, by whom?"—the connection is that he would give it into his hand. "Dehitā" means the state of possessing a body. "When Śaṅkara is enraged"—because of the burning of that body [by him]. In the second [verse], it says: "O Father, give me [the power] to bring him under my control. By what kind of splendor could I take away the fortune of my enemy? What could I do?
It is said that they were submerged in the ocean; by whom and for what reason was the earth raised up?
Of Hari in the form of a boar.

"What shall I do? is a question regarding an action; "of whom" means belonging to whom? "Vara" means excellent. "Āhava" means battle; [the phrase means] by that which nourishes or increases it. [This refers to] the splendor (*tejas*) of Hari. "Apahara" [is derived from] the root *puṣ* with the suffix *kvip*, and from the root *hṛ* with the optative suffix (*liṅ*). In the second [verse], [it means] by the form of the boar (*varāhavapuṣā*), i.e., in the shape of a pig, belonging to Hari.
What was done by whom when the ocean was churned? What was done by whom when the sea was churned? By whom was it churned?
The dialogue consisting of questions and answers, and the state of being the support for Vṛṣākapi.

"What? When the ocean was churned. Not as it was previously mentioned. Thus, the question is a statement of equal phrasing, and the answer is likewise. *Mā* means the moon; *mā* means prosperity (*śrī*). *Vṛṣākapi* refers to both Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu. What kind of water is in the lake in the spring? What kind of autumnal water is in the lake in the autumn?
The conversation was full of questions, and the reply remained unspoken from the face of the royal swan.

[Commentary]: *Kīdṛ* means "like a question," that is, equal to a question; just as a question consists of a single statement, so too does the answer. In the second [verse], the moon is the king, the swan is the sun, their feet are the rays, and their faces are the breaths; [the water] is struck by those winds. The moon asks: "In the autumn season, what is the evening like in the water?
And in the autumn season, what is the dawn like in the water? (44)
The white lotus that rivals the splendor of the sun, yet is beloved by the moon.

[Commentary: "Ask! [First interpretation: *Kamala* means a deer; because of its association with that, *kamalavat* refers to the Moon (*soma*). *Dhuta* means shaken off or dispelled. *Moha* means delusion or sleep. [The compound] refers to white lotuses (*kumuda*)—white water-lilies—in which delusion and sleep have been shaken off. O you who possess such white lotuses! Thus, "the evening (*pradoṣa*) has its white lotuses shaken off" (*dhutamohasitotpalaḥ*). This is because they blossom during the autumnal evening. [Second interpretation: *Kamala* means lotuses (*padma*). [The compound refers to] the supreme friend (*bandhutamaḥ*) of those lotuses.
"Hasitotpalah" refers to the dawn, because at that time the blue lotuses (*utpala*) appear as if smiling. In autumn—that is, at the autumnal dawn—the lotuses and blue lotuses bloom.
The illustrious one asks Hari: "Who indeed, of what appearance, and by whom was she given here; and for whom was she churned?"
Or how does a great warrior shine in battle, sword in hand, while shouting aloud? 45.
Bathing in the ocean of equanimity, which is free from agitation and delight.

[Commentary: "Śrīmān" means one who possesses *śrī* (fortune), such as Padmā and others. The connection is: "By whom, having been churned, was it given? This is a question regarding the action (*kiṃ kurvann*). "In battle" (*āhave*). How does the great warrior shine intensely while acting? In the first [interpretation], *mā* is Lakṣmī. One who exists together with me (*mayā*) is "samaḥ," such as Padmā and others. O "sama" (O you who are with her)! "Capalā" is Lakṣmī. "Samodā" means joyful. "By the ocean" (*sindhunā*) means by the Ocean of Milk. "Given to us" (*no 'smabhyam dattā*). In the second [interpretation]...

"Moving lightning"—he is equal to or like it. "With an upward toss"—that in which there is such an upward tossing; thus, he shines while brandishing his sword in such a way that it possesses moving lightning and an upward toss. Now, was it not the case that the question was posed in sequence by the words "the illustrious one asks Hari," and so forth? True; nevertheless, there is no fault. For when the meaning of a sentence is questioned, the answer is given in terms of the sentence as a whole, and there is no fixed rule for the order of words within a sentence. However, for the sake of the listener's ease of comprehension, poets who pose questions indicate the sequence for the respondent.
In some cases, for the sake of brevity in the composition or out of necessity, a deviation from the established order of presentation does not constitute a fault.
Here, [the author] asks: "Who remembers whom? and the summer, which is like a lamp signaling what is undesirable, asks: "O friend, where is it? What clothing is there?"
With eyes cast down and possessing little wealth, he asks: "Where does a being of infinite merit dwell, what is he like, and what does he cause to be done? (46)
The Jina is shrouded in darkness.

[Commentary on *ac-pṛ*]: The suffix *ac* [is applied]. The statement "the lamp is not desired" (*aniṣṭadīpa*) is for the purpose of prohibiting the recollection of a lamp. "Where, of what kind? means being of what sort in what place. "One with little wealth": for one who has much wealth would not go himself to the artisan. In the first [verse]: O *ac*! A man enveloped by darkness remembers the sun (*ina*). In the second: The Daitya named Andhaka; his enemy is Śaṅkara. O *ṛto*! Two Andhakas. *Ajina* is a garment of skin. In the third:
The two blind craftsmen [asked]: "O Jina, you who have yourself attained the Truth, what kind of Jina-image is this that you are having made?
Tell us, what is it like? What kind of arrival of clouds occurs during the seasons, and which one is it?"
Tell me, what kind of person is this younger brother of yours, who resembles a flock of swans upon a lake overflowing with water? (47)

O Cloud, among these seasons, which one is like you? Tell me these three things. Your younger brother is the autumn season (*śaratkāla*). It is called *samadasindhu* because its rivers (*sindhavaḥ*) are full of pride (*samada*) and swollen; it is so called because it exists together with the *kadamba* trees (*saha kadambair vartate*). In the second sense, *sindhurāḥ* refers to elephants, and *haṃsakadambakāni* refers to flocks of swans.
May that auspicious, stainless, joyful, and unafflicted weapon be for your protection!
May this discourse on the Dharma by the Sugata, the supreme sage, protect you!
Thus, O Wealth of Method, grant these two blessings to living beings;
may the scripture of the Great Sage, who possesses the ten powers, protect you! (48)

[Commentary: "Auspicious" (*śubha*) means praiseworthy, because it has selflessness (*nairātmya*) as its object. "Stainless" (*amala*) is so called because it is free from outflows (*anāsrava*). "Non-affliction" (*akleśa*) is the absence of afflictions; it is the destruction of afflictions, and it is also dispassion (*vairāgya*), since all afflictions are indicated by the term "attachment" (*rāga*). However, in this context, the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) which brings about that [dispassion] is metaphorically called "non-affliction. It is an "armament" (*āyudha*) by virtue of its power as a weapon. "Delight" (*moda*) is happiness, while "non-delight" (*amoda*) is suffering, characterized by cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). "That" (*sa*) refers to what is well-known.

The discourse on Dharma (*dharmavāda*) is the proclamation of the instruction on merit and knowledge. In the first [verse], there are six words: *sat*, *aśabalam*, *maharṣe*, *arāgam*, *astrāyatām*, *vaḥ*. It is "spotless" (*aśabalam*) because it is the antidote to faults. It is "free from passion" (*arāgam*), meaning the absence of passion. In the second [verse], there are five words: *saḥ*, *daśabalamaharṣeḥ*, *āgamaḥ*, *trāyatām*, *vaḥ*.
Sārahi says: What kind of speech could I not understand? I am not ignorant of the river that flows through the chest of Rāghava; who does not know the river that carries the flow of separation? (49)

[Commentary: Regarding *sāra*: In the first [verse], "O charioteer!"—even though she knows, the army (*vāhinī*) does not know how to fight, according to the maxim: "A slain army is like one made of non-metal. In the second [verse], Jānakī is one who carries the tears of separation; here, *vāhinī* means a river. O gentle one, tell me truly: is it by means of instruments or by chance that sounds are produced? Speak the ultimate truth; for the Dharma is free from attachment. (50)

[Commentary]: This is in Apabhraṃśa and in the *dvipadī* meter. Here, in the word *prāeṇa*, the vowel *e* should be pronounced as short (*hrasva*). As it has been said: "Filling [the measure] occurs through short, long, nasalized (*bindu*), quick (*druta*), and slow (*vilambita*) [syllables]. Generally, the phonemes associated with the seven musical notes (*svara*) in the *karaṇa* and *vartanī* are called *svaravarṇa*. How? Of what kind? O gentle one (*saumya*), that which is both dual—being the grasper—and non-dual due to the absence of its appearance, is non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*). One who is devoted to that is "engaged" (*rata*).

He delights in non-duality. Speak of the ultimate truth. First: seven steps. "Free from attachment to phenomena" (*pariniḥsaṅgadharmā*). Second: attachment is delusion, the perception of duality. Because that is absent, the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) are without attachment; they abide in the supreme state (*parasthāna*). The meaning is that others are inferior (*arvācīna*).
Bhīma asks: What appear as a sequence? Where in the new [state]?
Are they deer, porcupines, wrestlers, or those who possess only a single row of teeth? (51)

Bhīma: [The meaning is: "Are deer rivals to a boar? First: "Whose offspring is *kiḥ*? Bhīma, the son of Vāta. O *ke*! The cranes appear in rows in the cloud (*valāhaka*). Second: What wretched deer are there? In the boar (*varāhaka*).
O wise one who has conquered the heat of the summer days, do you take delight in the doctrine of the Jina? O *kiṅkita*!
O goddess, you rejoice here in the shade of this tree, your heart delighted by the falling rain of well-performed merit.

[Commentary: This is in the Paiśācika dialect. It is asked by Śakuni and by the summer heat: "O wise one (*budha*), for what reason do you take delight in the Buddha’s teaching? O god (*sura*), for what reason do you rejoice upon your own head? This is the meaning of the second question. "For what reason" (*kiṃkṛte*) asks about a specific action, not a substance. In the first [verse], there are three words: *suka*, *tapātapa*, and *sātaracarcite*. "O parrot" (*he śuka*), "O summer heat" (*he grīṣmātapa*): I take delight in the word of the Jina, which is contemplated with reverence (*sādara-cintite*).]
At that time, because the essence of its meaning was understood. Regarding the second [verse]: "I rejoice when my own head is honored and bowed by the dust obtained from the feet of the Sugata.
The Lord of Dharma asks: "Of what kind is it?
Where shall I perform it for victory? What is there? Whom?"
O Kalihāra, who here is laughing at what kind of young lotus stalk? 53.
May he who removes illusion, who delights in battle, and who wears the crest of Śiva, protect us.

[Commentary on *Vṛṣa*] "What shall I do? (*kiṃ karomi*)—this is a question regarding an action. "O you, O you, Hara!"—these words indicate a quarrel; for this very reason, the term *kalikāra* ("causing strife") is employed. The meaning is: what kind of child does the tip of the lotus-stalk mock? In the first [verse], there are four words: *mayaharam*, *samare*, *harase*, and *haram*. He is *mayahara* because he slew the demon named Maya in battle (*samare*). In the second [verse], there are three words: *mayaharaṃsaṃ*, *are*, and *haraseharaṃ mṛgadharāṃśam*.
[This refers to] the crescent moon (*candrakhaṇḍa*), which is the portion of the deer-bearer (the moon), resting upon the head of Hara.

"O sister, summon the Lord of Wealth, who is the master of the path and the leader of the caravan. "I am indeed the one heard by all, the wind that carries the fragrance; I am the leader of the caravan on the path. (54)

The one with the monkey-banner (Arjuna) struck down the ear of the enemy; [the commentary explains: *sadhana* here should be understood as the neuter form meaning "wealth" (*vitta*) and "lord of wealth" (*vittādhipa*). One who protects movement (*gamana*) is a *gamanapa*. Now, in the entire *gāndharva* [treatise], in brief, what has been heard? That is the meaning. It exists together with wealth (*rāya*), thus it is *sari*. Movement is *gama*; one who protects that is *ka*, so "O *gamapa*. One who possesses abundant wealth is *dhani*. In the second [case]: the collection of seven syllables is *sarigamapadhani*; the meaning is "the seven musical notes" (*sapta svarāḥ*). He whose ears were struck down by the enemy... the one with the monkey-banner.
Distressed, the Sun recalled [his vow] and asked:
"If you do not know, O friend, tell me then—who is who, what belongs to whom, and where? (55)
This great hymn, consisting of one thousand and eight verses, was heard by the son of Hari. (Pādottara).

[Commentary: *Niha* [means] "toward an enemy" (*arau*) who is "intolerant" (*asahane*). When Arjuna, the slayer of Karṇa, was being brought to mind, the Sun became distressed. What did he say? "If one rejoices when an insurmountable situation has arrived, then, O good man, speak! At that time, who [was] whose? For what reason? Upon what having arrived? [The six words are: *prathame*, *ṣaṭ*, *padāni*, *harisutaḥ*, *sutam*, *enam*, *ahan*, *na*, *me*, *hariḥ*, *indras*, *tasya*, *sutaḥ*, *arjunaḥ*, *sutam*, *me*, *karṇam*, *ahan*, *hatavān*. [Explanation: *Hari-sutaḥ* means the son of Hari (Indra), namely Arjuna. *Sutam* means my son, Karṇa. *Ahan* means he killed; he has slain him. *Na me hariḥ* means Indra is not mine. *Tasya sutaḥ* means his son, Arjuna. *Me sutam* means my son, Karṇa. *Ahan* means he killed; he has struck him down.

The sense is this: "Just as he was not an elephant, nor a deer, so too—O son of Jamadagni, O son of Kuntī—Karna has been struck down by six: by the Earth, by Vāsava, by you, by me, and by Kuntī. In the second [verse], there are four words: *harisu*, *tassu*, *tameṇa*, and *mahanname*. The meaning is: "His joy (*harṣas*) was [submerged] by that darkness (*tamasā*), like a great ocean (*mahārṇava*). It is well known that in the word *mahārṇava*, the letter *va* becomes *ma*. Furthermore, a nasalized conjunct (*ṇa-saṃyoga*) is also accepted as a nasalized conjunct (*na-saṃyoga*). For example: [Example follows: *...* (as per the source text)

The eightfold noble path is practiced; do not be one who lacks devotion. For whatever purpose Meru makes the sun his servant, that is gold. (Note: This is because the characteristics of Apabhraṃśa are not yet fully established.
[Apabhraṃśa stanza untraced]
Tell others to worship the Buddha; speak to others so that they may worship the Buddha.
Devote yourselves to this wise one, the crusher of the peak of Māra.

[Commentary: "The Buddha. [In the first line: "Worship this Victor (Jina), who has the luster of refined gold (ārakūṭaprabha) and the color of bell-metal (rīrīvarṇa); the wise Victor (dhīrājina), whose nature is to shine through wisdom (dhiyā rājanaśīla). [In the second line: "O wise ones (he dhīrāḥ)! Come here (eta); approach and worship the Victor who has shattered the peak of Māra (mārakūṭaprabhañjitam), whose nature is to destroy the illusions of Māra (māramāyābhañjanaśīlam).

One should say: "In that state where sensual desires are not fit for passion, neither on one's own ground nor in the sky; where the foremost stages are radiant; and where even the increase of suffering, disease, and wretchedness is difficult to find in existence—shake off that [existence]."

Where even the gods are unable to touch the ground with their fingertips due to the radiance from the crests of their crowns, who would not bow with reverence to the feet of the Victor, which must be traversed by them? Thus it should be said. || 57 ||
In this world, neither sensual enjoyments nor the radiant crowns of the gods are sufficient for passion; that which is free from fear and conflict, and honored by the virtuous, is what he desires.
The latter half.

In this world, who would not reverently bow to those feet of Gautama, which are worthy of passion, which reach up to the sky, which are the ground for the tips of the gods' crowns, and which shine like their crests? 58b.
The latter half.

*Commentary:* "Passions" (*rāga*): On which ground (*bhūmi*) are desires (*kāma*) not worthy of passion? Because they possess many defects. Where are those desires? In their own domain, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Nor are the radiant and most excellent grounds worthy of passion; "in the sky" (*khe*) refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), because it is entirely separated from the earth. "The sky" (*kha*) is the form realm. One should say: "Shake off—that is, destroy—that state in which there is the elevation of defects such as hardship. This is the meaning of the first question.

Where, while the gods are prostrating at the feet of the Jina, the radiance from their crowns is able to color the region of his toenails because it is uninterrupted. Of what sort [is that foot]? It is to be traversed by those gods; it is to be resorted to. Who indeed would not bow with reverence to that foot of the Jina? This is the meaning of the second question. The answer begins with "for passion" (*rāgāya*) and so forth. Regarding the first point: in this saṃsāra, sensual enjoyments and desires are not sufficient—that is, they are not worthy—for passion.

Because they are full of many faults: where are those enjoyments? In the downward realms, in the lower destinies, in certain regions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). And the radiant peaks of the celestial abodes in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are not sufficient for passion; for even those are subject to suffering because they are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). And in that saṃsāra, there is no lack of distress (*taṅka*), nor is there freedom from conflict (*raṇa*); and neither depression (*sāda*) nor disease (*roga*) is absent. "Lack of inclination" (*nati*) means becoming dull or weak; "distress" (*taṅka*) means hardship; "conflict" (*raṇa*) means strife; "depression" (*sāda*) means despondency; and "disease" (*roga*) means illness. This [is] his.

Having cast off that cycle of existence for me—[in the second verse: where, upon the feet of Gautama, which are to be properly traversed within *saṃsāra*—the gods, who travel through the sky (*nabhogāḥ*), perform prostrations; the splendor of the crests (*śekharābhā*) of those gods, [that is,] the radiance of their crowns, is sufficient to color the surface of the nails, capable of dyeing the ground of the toenails. Being full of reverence, who would not bow to those feet? The meaning is: everyone bows.
Remembering with wrath, "The Asuras are my enemies of the world," he whose vehicle is Garuḍa...
And you are a son of the Victor enriched by the six perfections; thus both [names] should be spoken. (59)
"The Dānavas are not to be slain by us, for they are always the enemies who strive for heaven;
yet you, O wise one of great heroism, shine while established in ascetic penance. (60a)
O wise one of great heroism, you shine while established in austerity— you who are incapable of being slain by the Dānavas and are always an enemy to those who obstruct the path to heaven.
The play of a single stanza.

[Commentary: Viṣṇu has Garuḍa as his vehicle. The son of the Jina is a Bodhisattva. Both of these should be spoken of individually by means of another word as "the one who shines" (*bhāsī*). The first [explanation] has the meaning of "uneven" (*viṣama*) in the subsequent [verse]. Thus the wise one, possessing such recollection, [says]: "O you of great heroism (*mahāvīrya*), you shine while abiding in wrath; you blaze in ascetic heat (*tapas*). A great bird is a *mahāviḥ*; that is, Garuḍa. By him, one is to be led—*īrya*. Or else, he whose movement (*īryā*) consists of going by means of him: the meaning is "having Garuḍa as his vehicle."

In the second [verse]: "O giver" (*dānavān*), by means of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*); "without malice, possessing ancient meditation" (*anavadhyānaḥ purātanadhyānaḥ*), by means of the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), because of carrying [beings] through successive births; "always in heaven, going to the next world" (*sadāsvargaḥ paralokagāmī*), by means of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), for his speed or flow is one of forbearance; "wise" (*dhīmān*), by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); "O you of great vigor" (*mahāvīrya*), by means of the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*). Thus, "you shine" (*rājase*) means that you blaze forth. Tārkṣya asks: "O Omniscient One, what is the destiny of those who harbor hatred?"

[Commentary on *kāme*: The term *aud* is a general designation for the roots *auṇṭ* and *auṇṭi*. That [root] undergoes the substitution *aut*. When the suffix *śnu* is present, of what is this a rule? Who is said to be renowned for his virtues? What would *kā* be when the king is exceedingly fierce? To whom is *kā* attached? Who is the wielder of the bow of the Lord (*prabhu*)? What is the long-eared one? Or rather, immediately after [the mention of] the bull (*vṛṣan*), let it be stated by what instrument, with Indra as the agent, the moon—bearing the mark of the hare—was made to have its characteristic mark.]

In the wheel with five compartments, marked with the name of the poet in the fourth enclosure and at the hub—meaning, in the six spokes, tips, and rims—the foot that is on the north [is the starting point], and that which is on the back is likewise [the end]. This is the meaning of the wheel-verse (*cakraśloka*). It brings fruit to all directions; that is, it makes them fruitful. "Śaśa" refers to the Bodhisattva born as a hare. Of whom? Of those who perceive virtues; the meaning is: of those who have faith in him alone as one who perceives virtue. Which hare is this?

By whom was his body offered as an oblation into the fire of his own splendor? To do what? To endure the pain of cooking; not to feel regret. Now, for whom was this difficult task performed by him? For a suitor who requested it. Of what sort was he? One whose form had grown old through effort—that is, for Śakra, who had assumed the guise of an aged Brahmin out of a desire to test his resolve to give away his own body. "Effort" (*yatna*) here refers to the activity of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).

Then the aged man, having attained that wonder, bowed down; thus [it was done]. He was one whose conduct (carita) was directed toward Indra (indraya). The suffix *śic* is used here in the sense of the reflexive object (*karmakartari*), resulting in *arañji*. If it is asked how he himself could be Indra, he says: "The self-controlled one" (*vaśī*). The sense is that, by virtue of his mastery (*vaśitva*), he himself assumed that other form; this is the intended meaning. The fourth quarter [of the verse] provides the answer. Its complete meaning should be grasped as a whole within the verse; its individual meanings are external. In its analyzed form, there are eight words: *śītām*, *śuḥ*.

One who has performed the defining characteristics (*kṛtalakṣaṇa*); by the breaker of strength (*balabhidā*); *ī*; *e*; Nāthasiddha; the moon (*śaśī*); the state of being cool (*śītām śībhāvam*); "Śu" means thus; because of the statement that the word *śṛ* is derived from the root *śru*; they know both the performed characteristic (*kṛtalakṣaṇa*) and the bestowed characteristic (*āhitalakṣaṇa*) as renowned through the perfection of qualities (*guṇasampadā*); by the breaker of the army (*sainyabhidā*); *ī* is Lakṣmī; *e* is Viṣṇu; the root *ṣiñ* means to bind; in the feminine, with the instrumental suffix *kvip*, it becomes *sit*; he bears the white (*sit*) of the Lord (*nātha*), thus Nāthasiddha; the moon is the hare-marked one (*śaśakī*); in the compound there are seven; the cool-rayed one (*śītāṃśuḥ*).

Marked with a sign; by the slayer of Bala (Indra); by whom; then; accomplished; the hare-marked one; the moon; marked with a sign; by Indra as the agent; by which hare as the instrument; "then" means: thus, when his body had been cast off, immediately after that [act of] wondrous love and respect, for the sake of establishing his fame, the moon was marked by him; the hare-marked one, the moon, became the "hare-bearer" (*śaśadhara*). [This is] the marking of the poet’s name on the fourth panel and the navel. It was composed by Ratnākara. [The commentary continues:
"One should speak elegantly; call out; remember; whose son did they say? Speaking thus... (vācyaṃ peśalam āhvaya smara sutaṃ kaṃ prāhatur bruvacī).

"What are you doing with the food? The cow is dripping with hunger. When has milk been produced?"—the answer to these questions is formed by the syllables "kuśalam" (well-being), using the third and fifth lines of the rotating wheel of six squares, with the feet moving in a circular path. [176]

"Transform it! [This is what must be said. "Elegant" means charming. "What are you doing? is a question regarding the action. "When hunger exists. Because of the complete knowledge of all phenomena in every aspect, there is awakening on all sides; thus, it is *saṃbodhi*. It has feet that revolve like a rim and possesses six compartments. That which has six compartments as its spokes is called "six-compartmented. Of such a wheel. The rest is easy to understand. The wheel is the meaning of the verse. This, for now, is a feat intended to amaze the wise.

Furthermore, since there is merit from this [work], what might its fruit be? To this he says: "Of living beings," and so forth. The word *punaḥ* (again/furthermore) has the sense of distinction. *Udbodhaḥ* means awakening, enlightenment, or instruction. *Mudam* means joy (*prīti*). *Balam* means capacity or power. Of what kind is it? *Anarthanut*: removing what is harmful; destroying that which is disadvantageous. *Ajayyam*: invincible, impossible for adversaries to conquer. For what purpose is it? For the sake of *bodhi* (enlightenment). How? Through *sadayatā*—the state of being a Bodhisattva—by which this fruit is to be attained.

Following that, step by step (*tadanupadam*). The root *yā* means "to reach. That which is this (*yat yeyam*). Where? In these stages (*bhūmiṣu*), such as the Joyous (*pramuditā*) and so forth. By what? By various powers (*dhāmabhiḥ*, i.e., *vīryaiḥ*), because they have different functions and objects. Swiftly (*laghu*), meaning quickly. Capable (*alam*) for the liberation of the world. By what for liberation? By the three vehicles (*tribhir yānaiḥ*). [The first half-verse consists of] five separate words: merit (*puṇyam*), this (*idam*), for the sake of the world (*jagadartham*), truly (*addhaḥ*), and merit (*puṇyam*). [The second half: "Delightful" (*manojñam*); *īḥ* is the god of love (*kāmadeva*), and his *daṃ* is his wife.

Born in that [place], O Īdañja! *Gadartha* means the purpose of speech (*gada*). From the root *ad*, meaning "to eat," comes *addhaḥ*. *Dhayaḥ* means "one who suckles"; the sense is "one who causes [others] to suckle. In the compound, there are three words: *jagadartha* means the welfare of the world; *tribhir yānaiḥ mokṣaḥ* (liberation by the three vehicles). "May my awakening be for that purpose"—this is the ellipsis.
